query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Short-range chemical ordering near grain boundaries in a compositionally complex, initially single-phase high-entropy alloy promotes local segregation and partial ordering states that embrittle boundaries under service-like loads, thereby reducing fracture toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized or solution-annealed, single-phase, compositionally complex alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi-based) with minimal second-phase precipitation and equiaxed grain structure.
generation.intervention: Combined experimental and modeling program: apply systematic thermal exposures (intermediate temperatures, varying durations) followed by multi-scale mechanical testing, atom-probe tomography, and advanced spectroscopy to quantify short-range ordering near grain boundaries and correlate it with fracture behavior.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant thermal and loading regimes, ranging from cryogenic to moderate temperatures under tensile or fracture toughness tests, ensuring stress states that may activate brittle intergranular fracture modes.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range ordering at or near grain boundaries leading to local compositional fluctuations and incipient boundary decohesion sites.
generation.mechanism: Localized ordering increases grain-boundary energy, facilitating boundary decohesion and intergranular cracking without requiring large-scale precipitation or pronounced segregation seen in many conventional alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the as-homogenized, minimally ordered baseline, samples aged at intermediate temperatures will show increased intergranular fracture and reduced toughness, while conventional alloys lacking such short-range ordering effects should exhibit relatively modest embrittlement under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: Fully solutionized, structurally stable alloy with minimal detectable ordering or precursor boundary segregation, verified by initial microscopy and mechanical tests.
generation.boundary: Embrittlement effects may become pronounced after extended operation times or repeated thermal cycling at moderate temperatures; outside these ranges, ductility and toughness should resemble the baseline state.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature-time-stress conditions and concentrations that trigger significant grain-boundary ordering remain undetermined, as do the kinetic rates of disorder/order transitions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare replicate specimens of the single-phase alloy and subject them to different annealing times at intermediate temperatures to induce short-range ordering near grain boundaries. In parallel, subject a conventional alloy to matching heat treatments as a control. Characterize boundary regions with atom-probe tomography and high-resolution electron microscopy, then measure mechanical properties including fracture toughness under tension at various temperatures.
measurements: Atom-probe tomography to quantify local boundary compositions
High-resolution TEM/STEM for detecting ordering or nanoscale clusters
Fracture toughness and tensile ductility testing under comparable conditions to track embrittlement
Fractography to identify intergranular cleavage features
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If grain boundaries exhibit substantial local ordering yet do not correspond to a clear drop in toughness or increase in intergranular fracture, or if similarly treated controls show comparable fracture modes and strength reductions, the hypothesis is not supported.

cited_evidence.text: Equiatomic multi-component metallic materials, referred to variously as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), multi-component alloys or compositionally complex alloys, have generated considerable excitement in the materials science community of late as a new class of materials that derive their properties not from a single dominant constituent, such as iron in steels, but rather from multiple principal elements with the potential for unique combinations of mechanical properties compared with conventional alloys. Much of the interest is predicated on the belief that many new alloys with useful properties are likely to be discovered near the centres (as opposed to the corners) of phase diagrams in compositionally complex systems. One of the extensively investigated high-entropy alloys, an equiatomic, face-centred cubic (fcc) metallic alloy comprising five transition elements, Cr, Mn Fe, Co and Ni, was introduced in 2004 (ref. ), although it was not for a decade that its mechanical properties were first systematically characterized. CrMnFeCoNi (often termed the Cantor alloy) displays strongly temperature-dependent strength and ductility with only a small strain-rate dependence. Furthermore, bet

These alloys can display excellent strength, ductility and toughness at room temperature, properties which are further enhanced or maintained at cryogenic temperatures where deformation nano-twinning becomes a more prominent mode of deformation. Despite our recent observations of various toughening mechanisms occurring on the nanometre length-scale in the vicinity of a crack tip in such an alloy, the quantitative strengthening effect from deformation twinning and the nature of twinning-induced plasticity remain somewhat uncertain. In this work, we show that the mechanical behaviour of the nominally equiatomic alloy CrCoNi, a medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with a single-phase, fcc structure, and even better mechanical properties than the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy—specifically, a high strength (∼1 GPa) and ductility (∼60% uniform elongation) combined with exceptional fracture toughness (KIc>200 MPa✓m)—can be related to its capacity for twinning-controlled deformation. Although recent experimental measurements of HAGB energy with this same alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) exist, a comparison of this prediction is difficult. Measurements of grain boundary energy are sensitive to thermally-driven grain boundary segregation (and possibly phase separation) of impurities. This value is relatively high for metals,, and may imply a propensity for localized cohesive failure or fracture at the boundaries. Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution.
